metadata.description: Master defensive bottom positions in BJJ. Complete guide covering survival tactics, frame creation, and escape fundamentals. 60% escape success rate.

overview:
The Defensive Bottom Position represents a critical survival state in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu where the practitioner on bottom focuses primarily on protecting themselves from immediate threats while creating opportunities to escape or recover guard. This position is characterized by being underneath an opponent who has established some form of control, requiring the bottom player to employ defensive frames, hip movement, and strategic positioning to prevent submission attacks and positional advancements. Understanding defensive bottom positions is fundamental to BJJ survival, as even advanced practitioners will find themselves in compromised positions that require immediate defensive action.

Defensive bottom positions encompass a range of scenarios from being flat on your back under side control, to being mounted, to defending against back control attempts. The unifying principle is the prioritization of survival and escape over offensive action. This requires practitioners to develop a hierarchy of defensive priorities: first protect the neck and prevent submissions, second create and maintain defensive frames to manage distance and pressure, and third work systematically toward positional improvement through hip escapes, bridges, and guard recovery techniques.

Mastery of defensive bottom positions separates practitioners who can survive against higher-level opponents from those who get submitted quickly. The position demands technical precision in framing, an understanding of weight distribution and pressure management, and the mental composure to work methodically through escape sequences even under significant physical pressure. Developing proficiency in defensive bottom play is essential for competition success, as it allows practitioners to neutralize opponents' attacks and create opportunities to transition back to more favorable positions.
state_invariants: Bottom player is on their back or side with opponent applying top pressure through chest, hips, or full body weight distribution across torso and shoulders, limiting mobility and creating control

Defensive frames are established or being fought for, with arms positioned between opponent's chest and defender's face/neck to create crucial space and prevent opponent from consolidating heavy pressure directly onto the head and upper body

Hips maintain some degree of mobility or are actively working to create movement, never remaining completely flat and static, with defender constantly adjusting hip angle and position to prevent opponent from settling their weight permanently

Head position is protected with chin tucked toward chest, preventing opponent from controlling the head or achieving favorable angles for chokes, with constant awareness of neck exposure and submission threats
prerequisites: Opponent has established top position with significant control advantage
Bottom player's guard has been passed or is in the process of being compromised
Immediate submission threat exists or positional consolidation is imminent
Bottom player needs to prioritize survival over offensive action
key_principles: Protect the neck first - establish chin tuck and hand fighting to prevent choke attacks before addressing positional concerns
Create and maintain defensive frames using forearms and hands against opponent's chest, hips, and shoulders to manage distance
Keep hips mobile and active, never allowing them to be completely flattened or pinned to the mat for extended periods
Work in systematic sequences - address immediate threats first, then create space, then pursue positional improvement
Maintain composure under pressure and avoid panic movements that expose additional vulnerabilities or waste energy
Use breathing techniques to stay calm and conserve energy while working through defensive sequences methodically
Recognize when to accept positional loss temporarily in order to avoid submission and create better escape opportunities

Opponent shifts weight to consolidate position

decision_tree.condition: If opponent is attempting a submission (choke or joint lock)

common_errors.error: Allowing arms to be trapped or extended beyond effective framing range
common_errors.consequence: Complete loss of defensive structure and increased vulnerability to submissions and heavier pressure
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to body, maintain bent arm frames that can absorb and redirect pressure while staying within recovery range

common_errors.error: Flattening out completely with back and hips fully against the mat
common_errors.consequence: Maximum surface area for opponent's weight distribution, making escape nearly impossible and allowing full control consolidation
common_errors.correction: Always maintain some angle with hips turned slightly, keeping at least one shoulder blade off the mat to preserve escape routes

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive, uncontrolled movements that waste energy
common_errors.consequence: Rapid fatigue, exposure of additional vulnerabilities, and loss of technical defensive structure
common_errors.correction: Work methodically through defensive sequences with controlled breathing, making deliberate movements based on opponent's weight shifts

common_errors.error: Neglecting to protect the neck while focusing solely on positional escape
common_errors.consequence: Exposure to choke attacks that can end the match before positional improvement is achieved
common_errors.correction: Maintain chin tuck and hand fighting awareness of neck protection as highest priority, only pursuing escapes after neck is secure

common_errors.error: Giving up on escape attempts and accepting the position passively
common_errors.consequence: Opponent gains unlimited time to improve position, set up submissions, and accumulate points without resistance
common_errors.correction: Continue working small adjustments and movements even under heavy pressure, creating cumulative effects that lead to escape opportunities

common_errors.error: Pushing directly into opponent's chest or hips without proper frame angles
common_errors.consequence: Wasted energy as opponent's weight advantage negates pushing force, while failing to create meaningful space
common_errors.correction: Use angled frames that redirect opponent's pressure to the side rather than trying to lift their weight directly upward

training_drills.name: Survival Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies mount or side control at 70% pressure. Bottom player must survive for 2 minutes using only defensive frames and hip movement without giving up back or being submitted. Focus on maintaining composure and technical structure under sustained pressure.

training_drills.name: Escape Sequence Practice
training_drills.description: Start from worst-case defensive position (flat under mount or side control). Work through complete escape sequence: establish frames, create space with hip escape, recover guard. Partner provides progressive resistance increasing from 50% to 80% as technique improves.

training_drills.name: Frame Fighting Drill
training_drills.description: Partner in top position attempts to break and pass defensive frames while bottom player maintains frame structure and replaces frames when compromised. Emphasizes constant frame maintenance and active hand fighting rather than passive blocking.

training_drills.name: Defensive to Offensive Transitions
training_drills.description: Start in defensive bottom position. Partner gives specific reactions (weight shift forward, posture up, reach for submission). Bottom player recognizes opening and immediately transitions to appropriate escape or sweep technique.

expert_insights.danaher: The defensive bottom position is where technical precision under pressure becomes most critical. The hierarchy of defensive priorities must be absolute: first establish structural safety through proper frames and neck protection, second create the mechanical capacity for movement through hip mobility, and third systematically work toward positional improvement. Many practitioners make the error of attempting to escape before establishing proper defensive structure, which results in exposure to submissions during the escape attempt. The key mechanical principle is understanding pressure vectors - opponent's weight creates force in specific directions, and effective frames must be positioned perpendicular to these vectors to create maximum resistance with minimum energy expenditure. Additionally, the concept of creating 'micro-spaces' is essential - rather than attempting large explosive escapes, focus on small incremental adjustments that accumulate over time to create escape opportunities.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, defensive bottom positions are where matches are often decided. The ability to survive under heavy pressure and systematically work back to guard separates winners from losers at the highest levels. My approach focuses on staying calm under pressure and recognizing specific patterns in how opponents distribute their weight. When someone is crushing you from top position, they're also limited in their mobility - every bit of pressure they apply in one direction creates a vulnerability in another direction. I always tell my students to feel where the pressure is heaviest and work movement in the opposite direction. Also, never stop moving your hips even if it's just small adjustments - the moment you accept being completely flat and static is when you've mentally given up the position. Competition-proven escapes from bad positions require technical precision combined with the mental toughness to keep working when you're exhausted and being pressured.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The defensive bottom position is where creativity and unconventional solutions can save your ass when traditional escapes aren't working. In the 10th Planet system, we've developed specific responses for when you're in the worst possible scenarios - completely flat, arms trapped, opponent heavy on your chest. The key is understanding that even from terrible positions, there are always options if you stay calm and think creatively. One principle I emphasize is the 'emergency escape protocol' - if standard hip escapes and frames aren't available, look for unconventional solutions like inverting, rolling to turtle, or even accepting a less dominant position temporarily to avoid a worse outcome. The Lockdown from bottom half guard is a perfect example of turning a defensive position into an attacking opportunity. Also, work on your ability to stay relaxed under pressure - tension burns energy and makes you easier to control. Learn to breathe, stay loose, and work technical solutions even when someone's crushing you.

metadata.title: Defensive Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Defensive Position in BJJ. Complete guide covering survival posture, frame creation, escape fundamentals, and guard recovery. Essential defensive skills for all levels.

overview:
Defensive Position represents the fundamental survival posture in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu when an opponent has established a dominant position. This conceptual position encompasses the core principles of protecting yourself from submissions, maintaining structural integrity under pressure, and creating opportunities to escape or recover guard. Rather than a single static position, Defensive Position is a dynamic state that applies across multiple bad positions including bottom of side control, mount, back control, and turtle. The primary goals are to prevent immediate submission threats, conserve energy, and systematically work toward positional improvement. Mastery of defensive positioning is essential for all practitioners, as it forms the foundation for survival against larger, stronger, or more skilled opponents.

The effectiveness of Defensive Position relies on understanding hierarchical priorities: first protect the neck and joints from submission, second create and maintain frames to manage space and pressure, and third establish movement patterns that lead to guard recovery or escape. This systematic approach transforms defensive situations from panic-inducing scrambles into methodical problem-solving scenarios. Advanced practitioners use defensive positioning not merely to survive, but to bait opponents into overcommitting to attacks, creating counter-opportunities and transitions to offensive positions.

Defensive Position is characterized by several key postural elements: tucking the chin to protect the neck, keeping elbows tight to the body to prevent arm isolations, creating frames with the forearms and shins to manage distance, and maintaining a curved spine to facilitate shrimping and bridging movements. The position requires constant micro-adjustments based on opponent pressure and attack angles, making it both a physical and mental discipline that separates experienced grapplers from beginners.
state_invariants: Chin tucked tightly to chest with neck protected, shoulders slightly elevated to create collar protection, eliminating space for collar grips or rear naked choke attacks
Elbows connected to ribs and hips, arms forming protective frames with forearms positioned between opponent's chest and your torso, creating structural barriers against pressure
Spine curved in defensive posture with shoulders off the mat when possible, maintaining ability to shrimp and create hip movement while preventing flat back exposure
Legs positioned strategically with knees drawn toward chest when appropriate, shins creating frames against opponent's hips or torso, feet ready to push or hook for escape movements
Weight distribution favoring one side to enable shrimping motion, with active hip movement to prevent opponent from settling their weight and establishing permanent control
prerequisites: Opponent has established a dominant position such as Side Control Top, Mount Top, Back Control Top, or similar controlling position
Immediate submission threats have been identified and prioritized for defensive response
Understanding of frame creation and maintenance under pressure using skeletal structure rather than muscular strength
Ability to maintain calm breathing and mental composure in compromised positions to enable technical execution
Recognition of escape pathways and guard recovery opportunities based on opponent's weight distribution and pressure angles
key_principles: Protect vital targets first: neck, arms, and joints take priority over positional advancement
Create and maintain structural frames using forearms, shins, and knees to manage opponent pressure
Keep elbows tight to body to prevent arm isolation and submission attacks
Maintain curved spine and avoid flat back positioning to enable hip escape movements
Breathe consistently and control panic response to maintain technical execution
Create small movements and incremental improvements rather than explosive escape attempts
Use opponent's pressure and weight distribution against them through timing and leverage

Opponent overcommits forward weight during passing attempt
Opponent shifts weight to isolate near side arm

common_errors.error: Flat positioning with back completely on mat
common_errors.consequence: Eliminates ability to shrimp or bridge, makes opponent's weight maximally effective, prevents escape movements and allows opponent to settle position permanently
common_errors.correction: Maintain curved spine with one shoulder slightly elevated, creating constant angle that enables hip movement and prevents opponent from fully settling weight

common_errors.error: Arm extension away from body to push opponent
common_errors.consequence: Exposes arms to isolation attacks including kimura, americana, and armbars, eliminates structural integrity of frames, wastes energy pushing against superior leverage
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows connected to ribs and hips, create frames with forearm bones perpendicular to opponent's pressure rather than pushing with muscles

common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to close distance and establish submission attacks, eliminates space needed for escape movements, creates panic response and energy depletion
common_errors.correction: Build frames with skeletal structure rather than muscle strength, adjust frame angles as pressure changes, create new frames before abandoning old ones

common_errors.error: Holding breath or irregular breathing patterns
common_errors.consequence: Triggers panic response in central nervous system, depletes energy reserves rapidly, impairs decision-making and technical execution, signals distress to opponent
common_errors.correction: Establish controlled breathing rhythm immediately upon entering defensive position, exhale during pressure application, maintain steady breath cycle throughout escape attempts

common_errors.error: Excessive strength application without technical foundation
common_errors.consequence: Depletes energy reserves without positional improvement, creates openings for opponent counters, reinforces bad habits, prevents development of proper technique
common_errors.correction: Focus on timing, leverage, and incremental movements rather than explosive strength, use opponent's pressure and momentum against them through proper positioning

common_errors.error: Chin elevation exposing neck to choke attacks
common_errors.consequence: Provides immediate access to carotid arteries and trachea for chokes, signals inexperience to opponent, creates submission opportunities from dominant positions
common_errors.correction: Tuck chin firmly to chest, create collar protection with shoulders, maintain neck defense as primary priority even during escape attempts

common_errors.error: Attempting large explosive escapes without creating proper frames first
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy on unsuccessful attempts, creates scrambles that favor opponent's superior position, potentially worsens position through failed escape
common_errors.correction: Build defensive structure methodically through frame creation, make small incremental improvements, time explosive movements for when opponent is transitioning or off-balance

training_drills.name: Defensive Posture Hold Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies gradually increasing pressure from side control while bottom player maintains proper defensive frames, tucked chin, and curved spine. Focus on breathing control and frame integrity under sustained pressure. Progress from static holds to dynamic pressure application.

training_drills.name: Progressive Escape Sequence Drill
training_drills.description: Start in worst-case defensive scenarios (flat under mount, back taken with hooks). Bottom player must systematically work through defensive hierarchy: protect neck, create frames, begin hip movement, recover guard. Top player provides realistic resistance at 50-70% intensity.

training_drills.name: Frame Creation and Maintenance Under Movement
training_drills.description: Bottom player maintains defensive frames while top player circulates around them attempting to flatten, isolate arms, and create submission opportunities. Focus on rebuilding frames immediately when one is compromised and transitioning between frame types based on opponent position.

training_drills.name: Escape Timing Recognition Drill
training_drills.description: Top player alternates between heavy pressure and creating space for transitions. Bottom player must recognize windows of opportunity and execute appropriate escapes (shrimp when space created, frame when pressure applied). Develops recognition of when to move versus when to maintain structure.

training_drills.name: Survival Sparring from Bad Positions
training_drills.description: Start each round in a different compromised position (side control, mount, back control, turtle). Bottom player's goal is to survive without being submitted and work toward guard recovery. Reset when guard is recovered or submission occurs. Builds mental toughness and technical problem-solving under pressure.

expert_insights.danaher: Defensive Position represents a scientific approach to survival based on understanding mechanical principles rather than memorizing specific techniques. The foundation of effective defense is hierarchical prioritization: neck and limb protection supersedes all other concerns, followed by structural frame creation, then movement initiation. What separates advanced defensive positioning from beginner survival is the concept of defensive layers - multiple redundant protective mechanisms working simultaneously so that if one fails, others remain intact. The chin tuck protects against chokes, the elbow connection prevents arm isolations, the curved spine enables hip movement, and the strategic leg positioning creates barriers against advancement. Each layer must be systematically dismantled by the opponent, buying time and creating counter-opportunities. Advanced practitioners don't just survive in defensive positions; they actively manage the opponent's attack sequence, controlling the pace of engagement and choosing which defensive layer to sacrifice strategically to enable escape movements.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Defensive Position in high-level competition is about energy efficiency and precise frame placement rather than pure survival. The key insight is creating what I call defensive wedges - frames positioned so they become stronger as more pressure is applied against them, similar to architectural buttresses. When you understand angle and leverage correctly, you can maintain frames with minimal muscular effort while the opponent exhausts themselves trying to flatten you. My defensive approach emphasizes creating brief moments of space through timing rather than attempting to maintain constant separation. When the opponent transitions or adjusts their pressure, that's when you shrimp, not when they're settled and driving forward. Competition-level defense also requires accepting small disadvantages to prevent larger ones - sometimes you give up the underhook to prevent the crossface, or you allow side control to prevent mount. Understanding these trade-offs and making them decisively rather than fighting every inch prevents the panic and exhaustion that leads to submissions.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Defensive Position within the 10th Planet system goes beyond traditional survival concepts into unconventional framing techniques that utilize leg positioning and inverted movements. We focus heavily on what I call connection disruption - rather than just building protective barriers, we actively work to break the opponent's established control points through unexpected angles and movements. The Lockdown from half guard bottom exemplifies this approach: instead of trying to create space through traditional frames, we use leg entanglement to completely change the geometry of the position, turning what appears defensive into an offensive control system. Our defensive philosophy also emphasizes transition through bad positions rather than static survival - using movements like the Electric Chair setup or Dogfight entries that move through compromised positions so quickly that the opponent can't capitalize on them. The mental aspect is crucial: defensive positions in our system aren't places to survive, they're temporary states you flow through on the way to offensive opportunities.

metadata.title: Defensive Top Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master defensive top positioning in BJJ. Maintain base and posture while preventing opponent advances. Critical survival skills with 60% retention rate.

overview:
Defensive Top Position represents a critical transitional state where the top practitioner must prioritize maintaining base and preventing opponent advancement rather than attacking. This position occurs when facing a skilled bottom player who has established strong frames, grips, or hooks that threaten sweeps or transitions. The primary objective shifts from offense to survival - maintaining top position while weathering the opponent's attacks and waiting for opportunities to improve position. This defensive mindset from top is essential when facing superior guard players or when fatigued, as premature offensive attempts can lead to sweeps or submissions.

Unlike offensive top positions where the practitioner actively seeks to pass or submit, Defensive Top Position requires patience, strong base mechanics, and situational awareness. The top player must distribute weight effectively to prevent being off-balanced, maintain proper posture to avoid submissions, and carefully choose moments to improve position without exposing themselves to counters. Success in this position relies on understanding weight distribution, grip fighting, and recognizing when to transition from defensive to offensive tactics. This position serves as a crucial bridge state, allowing practitioners to weather storms and regain offensive capabilities when opportunities arise.
state_invariants: Top practitioner maintains connection to opponent with at least one point of contact (hands, knees, or hips) while preventing full disengagement that would allow opponent to recover guard or initiate attacks

Base established through triangulated support structure - typically both feet on mat with knees or hands providing additional stability, center of gravity low and positioned to resist directional pressure from opponent's frames or hooks

Posture maintained with spine alignment preventing forward collapse into opponent's submission threats (guillotines, triangles) while avoiding excessive backward lean that exposes to sweeps, head position typically neutral or slightly forward with chin protected

Opponent on bottom has established defensive frames, grips, or hooks that create immediate sweep or submission threats, preventing top player from safely advancing position without first addressing these defensive structures
prerequisites: Established top position with opponent on bottom (from guard, half guard, or transitional state)
Opponent has created defensive frames, hooks, or grips that threaten sweeps or submissions
Recognition that offensive advancement carries high risk of being swept or submitted
Sufficient base awareness to identify and counter directional pressure from opponent's attacks
key_principles: Maintain low center of gravity with weight distributed through triangulated base structure (two feet plus knees or hands)
Keep posture aligned with spine straight - avoid leaning too far forward (submission risk) or backward (sweep risk)
Establish grips that control opponent's primary offensive weapons (collars, sleeves, legs) before attempting position improvement
Distribute weight strategically to counter opponent's directional pressure without committing fully to prevent sweep vulnerability
Maintain constant awareness of opponent's hip mobility and frame positioning to anticipate sweep attempts
Use small, controlled movements to improve position incrementally rather than large committal adjustments
Protect the head and neck at all times - chin down, head positioned to avoid guillotine and triangle entries

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts directional sweep with hooks or frames
Opponent breaks posture down attempting triangle or guillotine
Opponent establishes strong sleeve or collar grips for sweep setup
Opponent inverts or elevates hips attempting berimbolo or back take

decision_tree.condition: If opponent has established strong closed guard with broken posture and collar/sleeve grips threatening submissions
If opponent has butterfly hooks or other open guard configuration threatening sweeps with good frames
If opponent has half guard with underhook or lockdown preventing easy pass
If opponent has deep frames preventing chest-to-chest contact but no immediate submission threats

common_errors.error: Leaning forward excessively while attempting to control opponent's upper body
common_errors.consequence: Creates opportunity for guillotine chokes, triangle chokes, or arm drags as weight shifts over opponent's offensive weapons
common_errors.correction: Maintain upright posture with spine aligned vertically, using grips and base position rather than forward weight to control opponent

common_errors.error: Standing straight up with narrow base when opponent has hooks or frames established
common_errors.consequence: High center of gravity combined with opponent's leverage creates easy sweep opportunities in multiple directions
common_errors.correction: Keep low stance with wide base when standing, or transition through combat base position before fully standing to minimize sweep windows

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass immediately without first addressing opponent's primary defensive grips and frames
common_errors.consequence: Committed passing movements while opponent maintains strong grips lead to sweeps or back takes during transition
common_errors.correction: Prioritize grip fighting and frame removal before initiating pass, ensuring opponent's offensive tools are neutralized first

common_errors.error: Maintaining static position without making small adjustments to grips or base
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to slowly improve grips, establish better frames, and build momentum for sweep or submission attempts
common_errors.correction: Constantly make micro-adjustments to grips, base position, and weight distribution to disrupt opponent's offensive timing and positioning

common_errors.error: Posting hands on mat too close to opponent's body during defensive base recovery
common_errors.consequence: Short posting distance provides insufficient leverage to base out against sweeps, and hands within range of opponent's grip control
common_errors.correction: Post hands at least shoulder-width from opponent's body, creating longer lever arms for base stability and keeping hands out of easy grip range

common_errors.error: Crossing feet or legs while in opponent's guard
common_errors.consequence: Creates ankle lock vulnerability and significantly weakens base structure, making sweeps easier
common_errors.correction: Keep feet uncrossed with one or both feet flat on mat, maintaining triangulated base structure at all times

training_drills.name: Base Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Partner on bottom attempts sweeps from various guard positions while top player focuses purely on maintaining base and preventing being swept. Top player is not allowed to attempt passes, only defensive base work. Bottom player gradually increases sweep attempt intensity.

training_drills.name: Posture Recovery Flow
training_drills.description: Partner in closed guard repeatedly breaks top player's posture down while top player practices recovery mechanics. Focus on hip movement, hand positioning, and spine alignment during recovery. Progress from static to dynamic resistance.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting Specific Sparring
training_drills.description: Start from top position with opponent having strong grips and frames established. Focus exclusively on grip breaking, grip replacement, and preventing opponent from reestablishing dominant grips. Reset position after each successful grip exchange sequence.

training_drills.description: Start in defensive top position with opponent having strong frames and grips. Top player must first establish defensive stability, then identify and execute opportunity to transition to offensive passing when opponent creates opening. Partner provides realistic resistance with intentional windows.

expert_insights.danaher: Defensive top position is fundamentally a game of geometric stability versus directional pressure. The opponent on bottom is attempting to create angular leverage through frames, hooks, and grips that generate force vectors designed to compromise your base triangle. Your defensive priority must be maintaining a base structure that can resist multidirectional force - this requires understanding that base is not static but dynamic. As opponent pressure changes direction, your base must subtly adjust through micro-movements of feet, hips, and weight distribution. The critical error is remaining rigidly static, which allows opponent to build cumulative pressure in one direction until your base fails. Instead, think of your base as a suspension system that absorbs and redirects opponent's force through constant small adjustments. Only when you've established this dynamic stability can you begin to systematically address opponent's offensive tools - grips, frames, hooks - in a prioritized sequence that progressively reduces their attacking options. The transition from defensive to offensive occurs not through a single dramatic movement but through gradual positional improvement as you neutralize opponent threats one by one.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: When I'm in a defensive top position against a high-level guard player, my entire focus shifts to not getting swept - everything else is secondary. The reality of competition is that getting swept costs you points and momentum, and if your opponent is good enough to put you in a defensive position, they're good enough to capitalize if you make mistakes. My approach is simple: establish combat base immediately if possible, protect my head and neck from submissions, and make them work incredibly hard for every inch they want to advance their position. I'm not trying to pass right away - I'm trying to tire them out and force them to show me their attacks. Every sweep attempt they make costs them energy, and if I defend it properly with good base mechanics, I'm still on top and they've burned energy for nothing. The key transition point is recognizing when they're between attacks - that's when I can start to improve my position incrementally.
